newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed after Japanese, German comments.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed after Japanese, German comments.

text.p: The dollar surged above 1.80 marks on Tuesday for the first time in nearly six years but ended lower after German officials repeatedly said the dollar had risen too far.
It rose against the Japanese yen after a key Japanese official said the market was too optimistic about the yen.
The dollar initially rose against the mark, ascending to a peak of 1.8040 marks -- its highest level since August 1991 -- on fresh signs that Europe's proposed single currency will be a weak one.

The prominent German economic research group HWWA lowered its forecast for 1997 German gross domestic product growth, and said Germany's budget deficit was running higher than the target for entry into the planned single currency, the euro.

A Reuters survey showed European investors expect the euro to comprise a wide range of currencies, including many weaker units that would undermine the mark's status as Europe's leading currency, analysts said.

"The marketplace is saying the deutschemark is too high," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group, Ltd. "Until we see what will be the monetary policy for the new European Central Bank, it's hard to instill any confidence in the deutschemark."
But, later in New York trading, the dollar fell after Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler told reporters in Germany the dollar's rally may have become excessive.

Zeitler added that Germany wants a strong mark, and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel later told Reuters the German Cabinet will make a statement Wednesday endorsing a strong mark and a strong euro.
"Those comments seemed to drag the dollar down," said James Powers, vice president for corporate foreign exchange at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale.

The dollar fell to 1.7910 marks from 1.7955 late Monday, but rose to 115.45 yen from 114.00. The dollar fell to 1.4735 Swiss francs from 1.4753 and rose to Canadian $1.3705 from Canadian $1.3695. The British pound fell to $1.6795 from $1.6877.

The greenback rallied in Asian trading after Japan's vice minister for international affairs, Eisuke Sakakibara, was quoted on a news wire as saying the market's expectations of yen strength were too high.
Dubbed "Mr. Yen" for his currency market expertise, Sakakibara also said leaders of Japan and other major nations would not use foreign exchange rates as a tool to manipulate trade flows.
A stronger dollar, or weaker yen, would make Japanese products cheaper and more competitive on global markets, giving a lift to Japan's embattled economy.
"If Japan can keep the dollar a little higher against the yen, perhaps Japan's recovery can become a little more solid," said Malpede.
The steady flow of offical German objections to the dollar's gains prompted concerns that monetary authorities might enter the market to support the mark.
In fact, the Bank of Italy for the second straight day bought marks against the lira, dealers said.

"The German comments are suggesting that they are starting to really watch this and that they don't want it to get away from them," said Anjum Sayyed, currency dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.
